question: Your customer support agent handles returns, billing disputes, and account issues. After you revise its system prompt, a labeled evaluation set shows the correct-resolution rate rising from 91% to 95% overall. Billing disputes make up 6% of the set. A teammate concludes that the revision improved the agent's handling of every request type. How should you assess this conclusion?

options.text: Accept it, because a four-point overall gain on a labeled evaluation set is too large for any single request type to have gotten worse.
options.reason: A rise in the overall metric can still mask a drop on a small segment such as billing disputes, which the overall number cannot reveal.

options.text: Test it by rerunning the full evaluation set several times, and accept it if the overall 95% figure stays stable across all runs.
options.reason: A stable overall figure still says nothing about each segment, so a poor result on billing disputes can stay hidden in every run.

options.text: Treat it as unproven, because the overall gain can hide worse results on billing disputes, so compare accuracy per request type.
options.reason: Aggregate accuracy can mask poor performance on a specific segment, especially a small one, so the per-segment results must be checked before concluding anything about each type.

options.text: Test it by having the agent report a confidence score for each conversation, and accept it if the average reported confidence also rose.
options.reason: Confidence scores are useful only after calibration against labeled validation sets, and an averaged confidence figure is also an aggregate that hides segment-level problems.
